\subsection{Collapse Diagnostic Framework}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

Beyond its role as a pruning method, \rasp{} serves as a controlled perturbation that diagnoses how structural damage interacts with RL-based recovery. By comparing the GRPO training dynamics of models pruned with different criteria (importance-only vs.\ recovery-aware), we isolate the causal effect of functional redundancy removal on RL training stability.

\paragraph{Collapse metrics.}
We define GRPO training collapse as the state where the RL training process ceases to produce meaningful policy updates. We track four diagnostic signals per training step:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Mean reward}: the average reward across rollouts, reflecting exploration success.
    \item \textbf{Fraction zero-std} ($f_\text{zero}$): the fraction of prompts where all rollout rewards are identical, indicating loss of exploration diversity—when $f_\text{zero} \to 1$, the policy generates identical responses across samples.
    \item \textbf{Gradient norm} ($\|\nabla\|$): the magnitude of parameter updates—vanishing gradients indicate the policy is no longer being updated.
    \item \textbf{Mean terminated length}: the average length of naturally terminated (non-truncated) completions—collapse typically manifests as either degenerate short responses or max-length truncated outputs.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Collapse onset.}
We define collapse onset as the first training step $t_c$ where $f_\text{zero} \geq 0.85$ or $\|\nabla\| < 0.05$. Structured pruning reduces the cost of deploying reasoning language models, but recovery of pruned reasoning ability---particularly through Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)---is treated as independent of the pruning decision.
We show that this independence assumption fails: the choice of \emph{which} structures to prune determines whether RLVR-based recovery succeeds or collapses entirely.
We introduce Recovery-Aware Structured Pruning (\rasp{}), which uses intra-layer CKA functional overlap to score each structure as $S(h) = I(h) \times (1 - F(h))^\alpha$, preferentially removing structures whose computation overlaps with within-layer peers.
At 20\% structured sparsity on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, \rasp{} preserves 29\% GSM8K accuracy immediately after pruning versus 1\% for importance-only pruning ($p{<}0.0001$), and after SFT recovery reaches 61.49\% versus 59.29\% (+2.2pp).

\section{Conclusion}

We documented three findings at the intersection of structured pruning and RLVR-based recovery for reasoning models.
First, GRPO reward-accuracy decoupling is universal: reward improvement on the unpruned model (0$\to$0.661) produces zero accuracy change (81.27\%), and reward collapse on pruned models similarly leaves accuracy unchanged---the two signals are genuinely independent post-SFT.
Second, structured pruning induces GRPO training collapse whose severity depends on \emph{what} was pruned, not just how much: \rasp{}'s CKA-aware pruning collapses at step~10, six times faster than importance-only pruning at matched 20\% sparsity, directly implicating functional redundancy removal as the causal mechanism.
Third, these findings reveal a \emph{Redundancy-Stability Tradeoff}: functional overlap makes structures safely removable under SFT (their function redistributes via gradient learning, yielding +2.2pp over importance-only pruning), but essential for RLVR (they provide the exploration buffers GRPO requires for stable optimization).

The practical implication is that SFT-only recovery is the safe path for structurally pruned reasoning models; RLVR alignment of pruned architectures requires pruning strategies that preserve structural diversity rather than remove redundancy.
More broadly, our results extend the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis from ``which subnetwork trains well'' to ``which structures to remove so the remainder recovers well under a specific training paradigm''---a notion of \emph{paradigm-conditioned prunability} that implies pruning and recovery cannot be treated as independent pipeline stages.
